# Welcome

This tutorial walks through a complete **bulk RNA-seq** analysis on a real pediatric cancer dataset, **Wilms tumor** (the most common kidney cancer of childhood), with **limma**, one of the most widely used and best-documented tools for differential expression.

| Module | Question |
|--------|----------|
| **1 — Data and quality control** (this one) | What is in the expression matrix, and do the samples look the way we expect? |
| **2 — Differential expression with limma** | Which genes change between each child's tumor and their own normal kidney? |
| **3 — Gene set analysis** | Which biological programs do those changes point to? |

# Part 1 — The Dataset

The data come from **TARGET-WT**, the Wilms tumor project of the NCI's **TARGET** program (the pediatric counterpart of the adult-focused TCGA), downloaded from the **GDC Data Portal**. TARGET-WT has RNA-seq for 124 tumors, but only **6 normal kidney** samples. We keep exactly those 6 children, each with **two samples: the tumor and the normal kidney next to it**.

All files are in `data/`, built by `data-prep/build_target_wt_data.R` and `data-prep/build_paired_subset.R`:

| File | What it is |
|------|------------|
| `TARGET_WT_gene_expression_tpm.csv` | 19,938 protein-coding genes × **6 tumors**, in TPM |
| `TARGET_WT_control_gene_expression_tpm.csv` | the same genes × the **6 normal kidneys** of the same children |
| `sample_metadata.csv` | one row per tumor: age, sex, vital status |
| `TARGET_WT_control_clinical_raw.csv` | one row per normal sample, with the patient it comes from |

<div class="alert-info">
**Why a paired design?** Comparing a child's tumor with **their own** normal kidney removes everything that differs between children: genetic background, age, sex, how the samples were collected. What is left is the tumor effect. Six pairs is a small experiment, which is exactly the situation where limma's statistics (Module 2) make the biggest difference, and every step runs in seconds.
</div>

```{r load-data, echo=TRUE}
tumor_tpm   <- read_csv("data/TARGET_WT_gene_expression_tpm.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
control_tpm <- read_csv("data/TARGET_WT_control_gene_expression_tpm.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

tumor_metadata   <- read_csv("data/sample_metadata.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
control_metadata <- read_csv("data/TARGET_WT_control_clinical_raw.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

## TPM: What the Numbers Mean

Each value is a **TPM** (*transcripts per million*). For gene $i$ with $X_i$ reads and effective length $\ell_i$ (kb):

$$
\text{TPM}_i = \frac{X_i / \ell_i}{\sum_j X_j / \ell_j} \times 10^6
$$

1. **Divide by gene length**: a long gene collects more reads than a short one at the same expression level.
2. **Divide by the sample's total and multiply by one million**: removes the difference in sequencing depth between samples.

TPM values are already **normalized** and comparable across samples; summed over all genes, every sample totals exactly one million.

<div class="alert-info">
**TPM and the choice of method.** Count-based methods (DESeq2, edgeR, limma-*voom*) model the number of **reads**, and their statistics rely on the noise of counting. TPM no longer carries that information: the read counts have been divided by gene length and library size. For TPM, the appropriate approach is to work on **log2(TPM + 1)** with a method designed for continuous, approximately normal data. That is exactly what **limma** was built for (originally for microarrays), and Module 2 uses its **limma-trend** variant.
</div>

# Part 2 — Building One Matrix and One Sample Sheet

Tumors and normals arrive as two files. We combine them into **one matrix** (genes × samples) and **one sample sheet** in the same order. The sample sheet records, for every sample, its **condition** (Normal or Tumor) and its **patient**: the second column is what makes the design paired.

```{r combine, echo=TRUE}
# The two matrices must contain the same genes in the same order before being joined.
stopifnot(identical(tumor_tpm$gene_name, control_tpm$gene_name))

tpm <- as.matrix(bind_cols(tumor_tpm[, -1], control_tpm[, -1]))
rownames(tpm) <- tumor_tpm$gene_name

samples <- bind_rows(
  tumor_metadata %>% transmute(sample_id = case_submitter_id, patient = case_submitter_id,
                               condition = "Tumor", sex = sex_at_birth, age_years),
  control_metadata %>% transmute(sample_id = sample_submitter_id, patient = case_submitter_id,
                                 condition = "Normal")
) %>%
  group_by(patient) %>%
  fill(sex, age_years, .direction = "downup") %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(condition = factor(condition, levels = c("Normal", "Tumor")),
         patient   = factor(patient))

# The sample sheet must follow the matrix columns exactly: limma matches them by position.
samples <- samples[match(colnames(tpm), samples$sample_id), ]
stopifnot(identical(samples$sample_id, colnames(tpm)))

# Every patient must have exactly one tumor and one normal sample.
stopifnot(all(table(samples$patient, samples$condition) == 1))
```

```{r table-samples}
kable(samples %>% arrange(patient, condition) %>% select(patient, condition, sample_id, sex, age_years),
      caption = "The 12 samples: 6 children, each with a normal kidney and a tumor sample.")
```

<div class="alert-info">
**Reading the barcodes.** A tumor is named `TARGET-50-PALKCW`, its normal kidney `TARGET-50-PALKCW-11A`: same patient (`PALKCW`), sample type `11` = solid tissue normal. All six children have **Favorable** histology, the large majority of Wilms tumors.
</div>

# Part 3 — Sanity Checks

## TPM Totals

Our matrix keeps only **protein-coding** genes, so each sample sums to *somewhat less* than one million: the missing share is the sample's non-coding RNA. A sample far off the rest has an unusual RNA composition.

```{r plot-tpm-totals, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
tibble(sample_id = colnames(tpm), total_tpm = colSums(tpm)) %>%
  left_join(samples, by = "sample_id") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = patient, y = total_tpm / 1e3, fill = condition)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Normal = "#7f8c8d", Tumor = "#8e44ad")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Total protein-coding TPM (thousands)", fill = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1), legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Filtering Low-Expressed Genes

Genes that are essentially not expressed carry no information but still count as tests, making the multiple-testing correction harsher for every other gene. We keep a gene if it has **TPM ≥ 1 in at least 6 samples**, the size of one group, so a gene expressed only in normal kidney (or only in tumors) is still kept.

```{r filter, echo=TRUE}
min_samples <- min(table(samples$condition))
keep <- rowSums(tpm >= 1) >= min_samples

# log2(TPM + 1): the scale used from here on. The +1 avoids log(0).
log_expr <- log2(tpm[keep, ] + 1)
```

```{r table-filter}
kable(tibble(step = c("Genes before", paste0("Genes kept (TPM >= 1 in >= ", min_samples, " samples)"), "Genes removed"),
             genes = c(length(keep), sum(keep), sum(!keep))),
      caption = "Effect of the expression filter.")
```

## Why the log Scale?

TPM values span six orders of magnitude, and their variance grows with their mean: a few very highly expressed genes would dominate any analysis on the raw scale. The log transform makes fold changes symmetric (doubling = +1, halving = −1) and the distribution much closer to the normal shape that linear models assume.

```{r plot-densities, fig.width=11, fig.height=4.5}
bind_rows(
  tibble(value = as.vector(tpm[keep, ]), scale = "TPM"),
  tibble(value = as.vector(log_expr), scale = "log2(TPM + 1)")
) %>%
  mutate(scale = factor(scale, levels = c("TPM", "log2(TPM + 1)"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 80, fill = "#2980b9") +
  facet_wrap(~ scale, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Gene × sample values") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)
```

```{r plot-boxplots, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.5}
as_tibble(log_expr, rownames = "gene") %>%
  pivot_longer(-gene, names_to = "sample_id", values_to = "log_expr") %>%
  left_join(samples, by = "sample_id") %>%
  mutate(label = paste(str_remove(patient, "TARGET-50-"), condition)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = label, y = log_expr, fill = condition)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Normal = "#7f8c8d", Tumor = "#8e44ad")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "log2(TPM + 1)", fill = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1), legend.position = "bottom")
```

<div class="alert-info">
**What to look for.** One box per sample, with medians at roughly the same height: the normalization worked and no sample is grossly different.
</div>

# Part 4 — Principal Component Analysis

PCA summarizes thousands of genes into a few axes of variation; each sample becomes a point, and similar samples land close together. We use the **1,000 most variable genes**, centered but not scaled (all genes are already on the same log2 scale). A line joins the two samples of each child.

```{r pca, echo=TRUE}
top_variable <- names(sort(apply(log_expr, 1, var), decreasing = TRUE))[1:1000]
pca <- prcomp(t(log_expr[top_variable, ]), center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)

percent_var <- round(100 * pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2), 1)
pca_scores  <- as_tibble(pca$x[, 1:4], rownames = "sample_id") %>% left_join(samples, by = "sample_id")
```

```{r plot-pca, fig.width=8, fig.height=5.5}
pca_scores %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = PC1, y = PC2)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = patient), color = "grey70") +
  geom_point(aes(color = condition), size = 3.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = str_remove(patient, "TARGET-50-")), size = 3, vjust = -1.2, color = "grey30") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Normal = "#7f8c8d", Tumor = "#8e44ad")) +
  labs(x = paste0("PC1 (", percent_var[1], "%)"), y = paste0("PC2 (", percent_var[2], "%)"), color = NULL,
       title = "PCA, 1,000 most variable genes; lines join each child's two samples") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)
```

<div class="alert-info">
**How to read it.** PC1 alone explains **`r percent_var[1]`%** of the variance and separates every tumor from every normal kidney: tumor vs normal is by far the strongest signal. The six normal kidneys sit tightly together (a uniform tissue), while the tumors spread out: Wilms tumors mix blastemal, epithelial and stromal components in different proportions. The lines are roughly parallel: the tumor effect goes in a similar direction in every child.
</div>

# Part 5 — Sample-Sample Correlation

For every pair of samples, the **Pearson correlation** of their log expression across all kept genes: 1 = identical profiles. The heatmap is clustered, so similar samples appear next to each other.

```{r correlation, echo=TRUE}
sample_cor <- cor(log_expr, method = "pearson")
```

```{r plot-correlation, fig.width=8, fig.height=7}
labels <- paste(str_remove(samples$patient, "TARGET-50-"), samples$condition)
annotation <- data.frame(Condition = samples$condition, row.names = labels)
heatmap_cor <- sample_cor
diag(heatmap_cor) <- NA
dimnames(heatmap_cor) <- list(labels, labels)

pheatmap(
  heatmap_cor,
  color = viridisLite::viridis(100), na_col = "white",
  clustering_distance_rows = as.dist(1 - sample_cor), clustering_distance_cols = as.dist(1 - sample_cor),
  clustering_method = "average",
  annotation_col = annotation, annotation_row = annotation,
  annotation_colors = list(Condition = c(Normal = "#7f8c8d", Tumor = "#8e44ad")),
  annotation_names_row = FALSE, treeheight_row = 0, border_color = NA, fontsize = 9,
  main = "Sample-sample Pearson correlation (log2 TPM), clustered"
)
```

<div class="alert-info">
**Two blocks.** Normals correlate strongly with each other, tumors less so with each other, and normals with tumors least of all. A sample clustering with the wrong group, or correlating poorly with everything, would deserve a second look (RNA quality, tumor purity, a labeling error); none does here.
</div>

# Summary

- One matrix of `r ncol(tpm)` samples (6 tumors and their 6 normal kidneys) and one sample sheet, verified to match column by column.
- `r sum(keep)` genes kept after filtering, analyzed as **log2(TPM + 1)**.
- Tumor vs normal kidney dominates the data, and is consistent across the six children.

Module 2 fits the limma model.
